3.  Adopt an Ordinance Amending Chapter 9-5, Article 5 (L/M Low and Moderate Income
  -

  Housing) and Article 6 (Accessory Dwelling Units) of Title 9 of the Avalon Municipal Code,
  implementing housing programs 14 and 15 as set forth in the 6th Cycle General Plan
  Housing Element and Adoption of Exemption Findings Under the California
  Environmental Quality Act
  This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived during the September
  16, 2025 City Council Meeting. In September 2022, the City Council adopted the 2021-
  2029/6th Cycle General Plan Housing Element. The Housing Plan section of the Housing
  Element further sets forth the City’s goals, policies and programs to address Avalon’s
  identified housing needs. Some programs require one-time code amendments, while
  others have ongoing review schedules that require monitoring legislative actions and
  regular updates to the Avalon Municipal Code.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt an ordinance of the City of Avalon amending Chapter 9-5, Article 5 (L/M Low and
  -

  Moderate Income Housing) and Article 6 (Accessory Dwelling Units) of Title 9 of the
  Avalon Municipal Code, implementing housing programs 14 and 15 as set forth in the 6th
  Cycle General Plan Housing Element and adoption of exemption findings under the
  California Environmental Quality Act.

GENERAL BUSINESS

4.  Fire Department Mobile Incident Command Vehicle Replacement
  The City of Avalon was awarded a grant of $59,120 through Area F EMPG FY24 for a
  command vehicle replacement for an Emergency Operations Center (EOC). The goal of
  the funding is to upgrade mobile EOC capabilities so the City may be better prepared to
  receive and relay information during emergency situations.
  Recommended Action
  1. Per the City’s Procurement Policy, authorize the City Manager or his designee to
  execute an agreement with Watson Fleet Group for the purchase of a 2026 Chevrolet
  Silverado 2500HD, 4WD Crew Cab with 159” custom 6.9’ box by cooperative purchasing
  procedures. 2. Amend the Fiscal Year 25-26 Budget allocating $65,000 to fund 10245-
  6871, CIP Project Number 234501.

5.  Change Order #2 for Cultural Resources Consultation Agreement with Montrose
  Environmental Services
  The City entered into a professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental
  Solutions, Inc. (Montrose) to provide on-call cultural resources consultation services for
  the Five Corners Site Improvement Project. Montrose requested the City authorize
  Change Order #2 expanding monitoring efforts through December 2025 to coincide with
  the completion of the excavation phases of the project.

  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute Changer Order #2 for the professional services
  agreement with Montrose Environmental Solutions, Inc., to continue to provide cultural
  resource consulting for the Five Corner Site Improvement Project, for an additional sum
  of $50,000 and a new total contract sum of $216,128.00.

6.  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent Control Measures
  The purpose of this staff report is to provide the City Council with information on State
  law as it relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide examples of what other
  cities have codified locally so the City Council may consider what policy options it is
  interested in exploring for Avalon.
  Recommended Action
  Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control options available under State
  law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (“City”) staff to evaluate and report back on
  any desired local options available to the City.

7.  Adult-Use/Recreational Cannabis Discussion
  A member of the City Council requested City Staff pursue expansion of the Avalon
  Municipal Code to allow for the sale of adult-use/recreational cannabis in Avalon.
  Recommended Action
  Provide direction to Staff regarding City Council’s desire to pursue legalization of adult-
  use/recreational cannabis in Avalon.

  The following General Business item is the City Council acting as the Housing Authority.

8.  206 E. Whittley Retaining Wall Change Order
  Jordahl Construction, Inc. has been working diligently to build a retaining wall at the 206
  E. Whittley Housing Project. However, while working on the lower extent of the westerly
  side of the property it was determined the existing lower retaining wall at the property line
  did not have the required structural support for the proposed MSE retaining wall. A
  redesign effort has resulted in Change Order #1 from Jordahi Construction, Inc.
  Recommended Action
  1. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute a first amendment to the
  construction contract between the City of Avalon and Jordahl Construction Inc.
  incorporating Change Order #1 and increasing the contract sum by $270,000 for a total
  not to exceed amount of $987,255. 2. Amend the Fiscal Year 25-26 Budget by allocating
  an additional $170,000 to Capital Improvement Project #205015, Fund #15325-6547.

BACKGROUND: This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived during the
September 16, 2025 City Council Meeting.

On September 20, 2022, the City Council adopted the 2021-2029/6th Cycle General Plan
Housing Element. The Housing Element is a state-mandated section of the General Plan which
identifies the housing needs, opportunities, and constraints in the City of Avalon. The Housing
Plan section of the Housing Element further sets forth the City’s goals, policies and programs to
address Avalon’s identified housing needs, including production of 27 new housing units as
allocated by the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) Regional Housing
Needs Assessment (RHNA) for the 6th review cycle.

The Housing Plan contains 26 programs adopted to implement the goals and policies of the
Housing Element. Some programs require one-time code amendments, while others have
ongoing review schedules that require monitoring legislative actions and regular updates to the
Avalon Municipal Code (AMC). Over the next several months, the Planning and Building
Department will bring forth a series of code amendments for consideration to implement all of
the housing programs to ensure the City continues to be compliant with State law. The
amendments proposed at this time are intended to address the requirements of Program #14
(Accessory Dwelling Units) and Program #15 (Adequate Sites for Lower Income Households on
Nonvacant and Vacant Sites Previously Identified).

PROGRAM #14—ACCESSORY DWELLING UNITS: Accessory dwelling units (ADU5) and
junior accessory dwelling units (JADU5) help meet the City’s housing needs for all income
 levels and also provide a housing resource for seniors and low- and moderate-income
households throughout the entire community. In accordance with State law, accessory units
(also known as second units or granny flats) are allowed by right in all residential zones
within the city. Chapter 9-5, Article 6, Accessory Dwelling Units, provides specific
development standards and processing requirements for ADUs.

Program #14 requires that the City continue to amend the ordinance based on future
changes to State law and work with the California Department of Housing and Community
Development (HCD) to ensure continued compliance with State law. The City will also
continue to monitor the extent of ADU production to ensure that the ordinance modifications
are successful and that the Housing Element goals can be met.

SB 1211 and AB 2553, adopted in 2024 and effective as of January 1, 2025, are the most
recent legislative acts that include multiple updates to State ADU law which clarify the
development requirements for ADUs. Below is a summary of the amendments proposed to
comply with current State law requirements:

  •  Update Government Code and Health and Safety Code legal references throughout.
  •  Add definition for “livable space”. (Section 9-5.603)
  •  Clarify the number of detached ADUs permitted on a lot with proposed multi-family
  development. (Section 9-5.604.a.4)
  •  Clarify that JADUs are only permitted on lots zoned for single-family residences.
  (Section 9-5.605.a.3)
  •  Clarify the method of measuring the height of an ADU. (Section 9-5.605.b.5)
  •  Remove owner-occupancy requirement for ADUs constructed after January 1, 2025.
  (Section 9-5.605.g.1 and 2)
  •  Clarify that uncovered parking spaces are included in the types of off-street parking
  that do not need to be replaced when an ADU is constructed (Section 9-5.606.g.3)
  •  Add clarification of the number of allowed stories for an ADU. (Section 9-6.606.j)

In addition, Staff has reviewed the objective architectural design standards for ADU5 to
identify opportunities to clarify requirements and reduce impediments forADU development.
The following amendments are proposed to update the design standards for ADUs:

  •  Clarify the architectural requirements for window and door placement and privacy
  screening. (Section 9-5.606.h.5)
  •  Add architectural requirement that roof slope must match that of the dominant roof
  slope of the primary dwelling on a lot. (Section 9-5.606.h.7)
  •  Revise the requirements for site landscaping to require compliance with the objective
  standards of the underlying zone. (Section 9-5.606.i)

Complete amendment language is included in the draft ordinance (Attachment 1). It is the
opinion of staff that the proposed amendments comply with existing State law concerning ADUs
and fully implements Program #14 of the  Cycle Housing Element.
 PROGRAM #15  -  ADEQUATE SITES FOR LOWER INCOME HOUSEHOLDS ON
NON VACANT AND VACANT SITES PREVIOUSLY IDENTIFIED: As part of the Housing
Element development process, local governments are required to prepare an inventory of land
suitable for residential development, including vacant sites and sites having the potential for
redevelopment. During the preparation of the 6th Cycle Housing Element, one site on Tremont
Street (APN 7480-002-072) was identified as a housing opportunity site with potential to
accommodate the number of units required to meet the city’s RHNA unit allocation.

Program #15 of the Housing Element is intended to provide streamlined review of high-density
housing projects on the Tremont Street property which include affordable housing units. Program
#15 states:

  ‘The City of Avalon will rezone to allow developments by right pursuant to Government
  Code section 65583.2(i) when 20 percent or more of the units are affordable to lower
  income households on sites identified in Appendix A to accommodate the lower income
  RHNA that was previously identified in past housing elements. Specifically, the City will
  rezone the 1.52-acre nonvacant site located at Tremont Street (APN 7480-002-072)
  previously identified in the 5th cycle housing element.”

The Tremont Street property is currently zoned Low and Moderate Income Housing (L/M) and
is designated High Density Residential Community Housing in the General Plan Land Use
  —

Element. Pursuant to AMC Section 9-5.502, low and moderate income housing as defined in
AMC Chapter 9-1 1 is permitted by right in the L/M zone, and the maximum permitted density is
40 dwelling units per acre. Therefore, the property is already appropriately zoned for compliance
with Program 15.

To further clarify implementation of Program #15, Staff proposed that a new AMC Section 9-
5.505 be added to Chapter 9-5, Article 5 of Title 9 (L/M Low and Moderate Income Housing),

which states that residential development on the Tremont Street property shall be considered a
by-right use, and may be processed without discretionary review, when at least 20 percent or
more of units are reserved for affordable to low and very low income households and the project
has a density of at least 30 dwelling units per acre. Complete amendment language is included
in the draft ordinance (Attachment 1).

It is the opinion of staff that the proposed amendments L/M zone fully implement Program #15
of the Housing Element.The Tremont Street property is owned by the Santa Catalina Island
Company and is already partially developed with residential units. In compliance Program #15,
if the City receives an application for a housing development project during this cycle, the City
will notify HCD and process the application consistent with State law.

PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS: On September 3, 2025, the Planning
Commission held a duly noticed public hearing at which time written and oral evidence was
considered regarding the proposed amendments. The Planning Commission adopted Planning
Commission Resolution No. 25-49, which recommends adoption of the proposed ordinance by
the City Council, with the following additional recommendations regarding off-street parking
requirements for ADUs and JADUs:
   •  Access to the City of Avalon Seaside Transit (COAST) transit system shall be considered
  as public transit for the purpose of applying exemption criteria from providing off-street
  parking spaces for ADU5 and JADU5.

AMC Section 9-5.606.g provides several possible exemptions from providing off-street parking
for ADUs and JADUs, as provided by State law. Specifically, AMC Section 9-5.606.g.a states
that no off-street parking space is required when the ADU is located within one-half mile walking
distance of public transit, as defined by AMC Section 9-5.603.

The definition of “public transit” in AMC Section 9-5.603 is based on the Government Code
definition for public transit as set forth in Gov Code Section 66313(m), which defines public
transit as “a location, including, but not limited to, a bus stop or train station, where the public
may access buses, trains, subways, and other forms of transportation that charge set fares, run
on fixed routes, and are available to the public”. COAST does not meet the State definition of
public transit, as it operates as an on-demand service and does not run on a fixed route.

The Planning Commission recommends that due to the unique nature of COAST as an on-
demand transit system, that the applicable AMC section be amended to incorporate COAST as
a qualifier for the ADU parking exemption criteria.

It is the opinion of staff that expanding the definition of “public transit” to include COAST on-
demand transit system does not conflict with State law, as the City is expanding opportunities to
eliminate off-street parking requirements. This is consistent with the intent of applicable State
law for ADU parking regulations that intend to decrease barriers to the construction of ADUs.
Therefore, staff has updated the definition of “public transit” in AMC Section 9-5.603, and the
amended language is reflected in the draft ordinance and strike-through amendment text. As
proposed, nearly all residential properties within the city will qualify for a parking exemption as
long as they have access to the public right-of-way.

  •  Should a property owner wish to acquire an autoette vehicle permit for the ADU/JADU,
  then the property would be required to provide off-street parking to be eligible for an
  autoette vehicle permit.

At this time, ADUs and JADU5 are not eligible for autoette permits pursuant to AMC Section 4.4-
1703.g.9. However, the ADU regulations currently require that an off-street parking space be
provided regardless, unless one of the parking space exemption criteria are met. To bring the
parking space requirements and vehicle permit qualifications into alignment, Planning
Commission recommended that if the residents of an ADU wished to have a vehicle permit, then
appropriate off-street parking should be required to reduce on-street parking congestion.
Otherwise, off-street parking should not be required in order to lessen the development
constraints for new ADUs.

At the March 4, 2025, regular meeting, the City Council provided direction to staff to consider
revisions to the vehicle code to allow ADUs to be granted autoette permits, so long as
 appropriate off-street parking is provided for the vehicle. Therefore, the Planning Commission’s
recommendation is in line with previous direction provided by the City Council.

Staff has added the recommended off-street parking exemption language as AMC Section 9-
5.606.g.2.g in both the draft ordinance and strike-through amendment text. Ad proposed, ADUs
shall be exempt from providing off-street parking unless the resident or owner maintains a valid
autoette permit for the unit. However, a separate text amendment to AMC Section 4.4-1703.g.9
is required before any ADU or JADU resident may apply for an autoette permit, which City
Council may undertake as a separate action.

Section 4. CEQA Exemptions.
The ordinance is exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental Quality Act

The General Plan is a long-term policy guide for the development of the City but does not
propose specific development that can be analyzed at a project-specific level. Therefore,
the General Plan EIR is a Program EIR (State Clearinghouse No. 2011091042). A
Program EIR provides a more general analysis of the General Plan that focuses on the
overall effects of implementation of the General Plan. The  Cycle General Plan Housing
Element was adopted in September 2022. An addendum to the Program EIR was
prepared which concluded that the Housing Element updates do not result in any new or
greater environmental impacts than were previously analyzed, disclosed, and mitigated.

Pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21083.3 and CEQA Guideline 15183(a), a
project that is consistent with the development densities established in a General Plan for
which an EIR was certified is not required to undergo additional environmental review
“except as might be necessary to examine whether there are project-specific significant
effects which are peculiar to the project or its site.” As noted above, an EIR was certified
for the General Plan. The amendments contained in the ordinance do not authorize
construction and make minor changes to existing standards and land use limitations that
apply to existing uses permitted in residential zones in the City and allow uses that are
consistent with the residential uses currently permitted in such zones.

In addition, Guideline 1 5061(b)(3) states that a project is exempt from CEQA if the activity
covered by the common sense exemption that CEQA only applies to projects which have
 the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment. The amendments provide
standards for the approval of allowed growth within the parameters of existing General
Plan and municipal code regulations. It does not authorize any changes to land use
limitations or approve any new development project. Therefore, there is no reasonable
possibility that the activity in question may have a significant effect on the environment.

Further, California Public Resources Code section 21080.17 provides that the California
Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) does not apply to the adoption of an ordinance by a
city or county implementing the provisions of Section 65852.1 or Section 65852.2 of the
Government Code, which is California’s ADU law and which also regulates JADUs, as
defined by section 66313. Therefore, the component of the ordinance which implements
state ADU law is statutorily exempt from CEQA.

Therefore, it can be seen with certainty that the ordinance has no potential to cause a
significant effect on the environment, and the amendments themselves are categorically
exempt from further review under CEQA pursuant to Sections 15183(a) and 15061 (b)(3)
of the California Code of Regulations.

§ 9-5.604 Approvals.
The following approvals apply to ADUs and JADUs under this section:
(a) Building-permit Only. If an ADU or JADU complies with each of the general
requirements in subsection 9-5.605 below, it is allowed with only a building permit in the
following scenarios:
  (1) Converted on Single-family Lot: One ADU as described in this subsection 9-
  5.604(a)(1) and one JADU on a lot with a proposed or existing single-family
  dwelling on it, where the ADU or JADU:
  a. Is either: within the space of a proposed single-family dwelling; within
  the existing space of an existing single-family dwelling; or (in the case of
  an ADU only) within the existing space of an accessory structure, plus up
  to 150 additional square feet if the expansion is limited to accommodating
  ingress and egress; and
  b. Has exterior access that is independent of that for the single-family
  dwelling; and
  c. Has side and rear setbacks sufficient for fire and safety, as dictated by
  applicable building and fire codes.
  d. The JADU complies with the requirements of Government Code
  sections 66333 through 66339.
  (2) Limited Detached on Single-family Lot: One detached, new-construction ADU
  on a lot with a proposed or existing single-family dwelling (in addition to any JADU
  that might otherwise be established on the lot under subsection 9-
  5.604(a)(1) above), if the detached ADU satisfies each of the following limitations:
  a. The side- and rear-yard setbacks are at least three feet.
  b. The total floor area is 800 square feet or smaller.
   c. The peak height above grade does not exceed the applicable height limit
  in subsection 9-5.605(b) below.
  (3) Converted on Multifamily Lot: One or more ADUs within portions of existing
  multifamily dwelling structures that are not used as livable space, including but
  not limited to storage rooms, boiler rooms, passageways, attics, basements, or
  garages, if each converted ADU complies with state building standards for
  dwellings. Under this subsection 9-5.604(a)(3), at least one converted ADU is
  allowed within an existing multifamily dwelling, up to a quantity equal to 25% of
  the existing multifamily dwelling units.
  (4) Limited Detached on Multifamily Lot: No more than two detached ADUs on a
  lot with a proposed multifamily dwelling, or up to eight detached ADUs on a lot
  with an existing multifamily dwelling, if each detached ADU satisfies all of the
  following limitations:
  a. The side- and rear-yard setbacks are at least three feet. If the existing
  multifamily dwelling has a rear or side yard setback of less than four feet,
  the City will not require any modification to the multifamily dwelling as a
  condition of approving the ADU.
  b. The peak height above grade does not exceed the applicable height
  limit provided in subsection 9-5.605(b) below.
  c. If the lot has an existing multifamily dwelling, the quantity of detached
  ADUs does not exceed the number of primary dwelling units on the lot.
(b) ADU Permit.
  (1) Except as allowed under subsection 9-5.604(a) above, no ADU may be
  created without a building permit and an ADU permit in compliance with the
  standards set forth in subsections 9-5.605 and 9-5.606 below.
  (2) The City may charge a fee to reimburse it for costs incurred in processing ADU
  permits, including the costs of adopting or amending the City’s ADU ordinance.
  The ADU-permit processing fee is determined by the Director of Community
  Development and approved by the City Council by resolution.
(c) Process and Timing.
  (1) An ADU permit is considered and approved ministerially, without discretionary
  review or a hearing.
  (2) The City must approve or deny an application to create an ADU or JADU within
  60 days from the date that the City receives a completed application. If the City
  has not approved or denied the completed application within 60 days, the
  application is deemed approved unless either:
  a. The applicant requests a delay, in which case the 60-day time period is
  tolled for the period of the requested delay, or
  b. When an application to create an ADU or JADU is submitted with a
   permit application to create a new single-family or multifamily dwelling on
  the lot, the City may delay acting on the permit application for the ADU or
  JADU until the City acts on the permit application to create the new single-
  family or multifamily dwelling, but the application to create the ADU or
  JADU will still be considered ministerially without discretionary review or a
  hearing.
  (3) If the City denies an application to create an ADU or JADU, the City must
  provide the applicant with comments that include, among other things, a list of all
  the defective or deficient items and a description of how the application may be
  remedied by the applicant. Notice of the denial and corresponding comments
  must be provided to the applicant within the 60-day time period established by
  subsection 9-5.604(c)(2) above.
  (4) A demolition permit for a detached garage that is to be replaced with an ADU
  is reviewed with the application for the ADU and issued at the same time.

§ 9-5.605 General ADU and JADU Requirements.
The following requirements apply to all ADUs and JADUs that are approved under
subsections 9-5.604(a) or 9-5.604(b) above:
(a) Zoning.
  (1) An ADU or JADU subject only to a building permit under subsection 9-604(a)
  above may be created on a lot in a residential or mixed-use zone.
  (2) An ADU or JADU subject to an ADU permit under subsection 9-
  5.604(b) above may be created on a lot that is zoned to allow single-family
  dwelling residential use or multifamily dwelling residential use.
  (3) In accordance with Government Code section 66333(a), a JADU may only be
  created on a lot zoned for single-family residences.
(b) Height.
  (1) Except as otherwise provided by subsections 9-5.605(b)(2) and 9-
  5.605(b)(3) below, a detached ADU created on a lot with an existing or proposed
  single family or multifamily dwelling unit may not exceed 16 feet in height.
  (2) A detached ADU may be up to 18 feet in height if it is created on a lot with an
  existing or proposed single family or multifamily dwelling unit that is located within
  one-half mile walking distance of a major transit stop or a high quality transit
  corridor, as those terms are defined in Section 21155 of the Public Resources
  Code, and the ADU may be up to two additional feet in height (for a maximum of
  20 feet) if necessary to accommodate a roof pitch on the ADU that is aligned with
  the roof pitch of the primary dwelling unit.
  (3) A detached ADU created on a lot with an existing or proposed multifamily
  dwelling that has more than one story above grade may not exceed 18 feet in
   height.
  (4) An ADU that is attached to the primary dwelling may not exceed 25 feet in
  height or the height limitation imposed by the underlying zone that applies to the
  primary dwelling, whichever is lower. Notwithstanding the foregoing, ADUs
  subject to this subsection 9-5.605(b)(4) may not exceed two stories.
  (5) For purposes of this subsection 9-5.605(b), height is measured from existing
  legal grade or the level of the lowest floor, whichever is lower, to the peak of the
  structure.
(c) Fire Sprinklers.
  (1) Fire sprinklers are required in an ADU if sprinklers are required in the primary
  residence.
  (2) The construction of an ADU does not trigger a requirement for fire sprinklers
  to be installed in the existing primary dwelling.
(d) Rental Term. No ADU or JADU may be rented for a term that is shorter than 30 days.
This prohibition applies regardless of when the ADU or JADU was created.
(e) No Separate Conveyance. An ADU or JADU may be rented, but, except as otherwise
provided in Government Code Section 66341, no ADU or JADU may be sold or
otherwise conveyed separately from the lot and the primary dwelling (in the case of a
single-family lot) or from the lot and all of the dwellings (in the case of a multifamily lot).
(f) Septic System. If the ADU or JADU will connect to an onsite wastewater-treatment
system, the owner must include with the application a percolation test completed within
the last five years or, if the percolation test has been recertified, within the last 10 years.
(g) Owner Occupancy.
  (1) ADUs created under this section on or after January 1, 2020 are not subject
  to any owner-occupancy requirement.
  (2) As required by state law, all JADUs are subject to an owner-occupancy
  requirement. A natural person with legal or equitable title to the property must
  reside on the property, in either the primary dwelling or JADU, as the person’s
  legal domicile and permanent residence. However, the owner-occupancy
  requirement in this subsection 9-5.605(g)(3) does not apply if the property is
  entirely owned by another governmental agency, land trust, or housing
  organization.
(h) Deed Restriction. Prior to issuance of a building permit for an ADU or JADU, a deed
restriction must be recorded against the title of the property in the County Recorder’s
office and a copy filed with the Director (or their designee) and filed with the Planning
Department. The deed restriction must run with the land and bind all future owners. The
form of the deed restriction will be provided by the City and must provide that:
  (1) Except as otherwise provided in Government Code Section 66341, the ADU
  or JADU may not be sold separately from the primary dwelling.
   (2) The ADU or JADU is restricted to the approved size and to other attributes
  allowed by this section.
  (3) The deed restriction runs with the land and may be enforced against future
  property owners.
  (4) The deed restriction may be removed if the owner ehminates the ADU or
  JADU, as evidenced by, for example, removal of the kitchen facilities. To remove
  the deed restriction, an owner may make a written request of the Director,
  providing evidence that the ADU or JADU has in fact been eliminated. The
  Director may then determine whether the evidence supports the claim that the
  ADU or JADU has been eliminated. Appeal may be taken from the Director’s
  determination consistent with other provisions of this Code. If the ADU or JADU
  is not entirely physicaHy removed, but is only eliminated by virtue of having a
  necessary component of an ADU or JADU removed, the remaining structure and
  improvements must otherwise comply with applicable provisions of this Code.
  (5) The deed restriction is enforceable by the Director or his or her designee for
  the benefit of the City. Failure of the property owner to comply with the deed
  restriction may result in legal action against the property owner, and the City is
  authorized to obtain any remedy available to it at law or equity, including, but not
  limited to, obtaining an injunction enjoining the use of the ADU or JADU in
  violation of the recorded restrictions or abatement of the illegal unit.
(i) Income Reporting. In order to facilitate the City’s obligation to identify adequate sites
for housing in accordance with Government Code sections 65583.1 and 66330, the
following requirements must be satisfied:
  (1) With the building-permit application, the applicant must provide the City with
  an estimate of the projected annualized rent that will be charged for the ADU or
  JADU.
  (2) Within 90 days after each January lof the issuance of the building permit, the
  owner must report the actual rent charged for the ADU or JADU during the prior
  year. If the City does not receive the report within the 90-day period, the owner is
  in violation of this Code, and the City may send the owner a notice of violation
  and allow the owner another 30 days to submit the report. If the owner fails to
  submit the report within the 30-day period, the City may enforce this provision in
  accordance with applicable law.

U) Building & Safety.
  (1) Must comply with building code. Subject to subsection 9-5.605(j)(2) below, all
  ADUs and JADUs must comply with all local building code requirements.
  (2) No change of occupancy. Construction of an ADU does not constitute a Group
  R occupancy change under the local building code, as described in Section 310
  of the California Building Code, unless the building official or Code Enforcement
  Officer makes a written finding based on substantial evidence in the record that
  the construction of the ADU could have a specific, adverse impact on public health
   and safety. Nothing in this subsection 9-5.605(j)(2) prevents the City from
  changing the occupancy code of a space that was uninhabitable space or that
  was only permitted for nonresidential use and was subsequently converted for
  residential use in accordance with this section.

§ 9-5.606 Specific ADU Requirements.
The following requirements apply only to ADUs that require an ADU permit under
subsection 9-5.604(b) above.
(a) Maximum Size.
  (1) The maximum size of a detached or attached ADU subject to this
  subsection 9-5.606 is 850 square feet for a studio or one-bedroom unit and 1,000
  square feet for a unit with two or more bedrooms.
  (2) An attached ADU that is created on a lot with an existing primary dwelling is
  further limited to 50% of the floor area of the existing primary dwelling.
  (3) Application of other development standards in this subsection 9-5.606, such
  as FAR or lot coverage, might further limit the size of the ADU, but no application
  of the percent-based size limit in subsection 9-5.606(a)(2) above or of an FAR,
  front setback, lot coverage limit, or open-space requirement may require the ADU
  to be less than 800 square feet.
(b) Floor Area Ratio (FAR). No ADU subject to this subsection 9-5.606 may cause the
total FAR of the lot to exceed 45%, subject to subsection 9-5.606(a)(3) above.
(c) Setbacks.
  (1) An ADU that is subject to this subsection 9-5.606 must conform to a 3-foot
  front-yard setback, subject to subsection 9-5.606(a)(3) above.
  (2) An ADU that is subject to this subsection 9-5.606 must conform to 3-foot side-
  and rear-yard setbacks.
  (3) No setback is required for an ADU that is subject to this subsection 9-5.606 if
  the ADU is constructed in the same location and to the same dimensions as an
  existing structure.
(d) Lot Coverage. No ADU subject to this subsection 9-5.606 may cause the total lot
coverage of the lot to exceed 50%, subject to subsection 9-5.606(a)(3) above.
(e) Minimum Open Space. No ADU subject to this subsection 9-5.606 may cause the
total percentage of open space of the lot to fall below 50%, subject to subsection 9-
5.606(a)(3) above.
(f) Passageway. No passageway, as defined by subsection 9-5.603 above, is required
for an ADU.
(g) Parking.
   (1) Generally. One off-street parking space is required for each ADU. The parking
  space may be provided in setback areas or as tandem parking, as defined by
  subsection 9-5.603 above.
  (2) Exceptions. No parking under subsection 9-5.606(g)(1) is required in the
  following situations:
  a. The ADU is located within one-half mile walking distance of public
  transit, as defined in subsection 9-5.603 above.
  b. The ADU is located within an architecturally and historically significant
  historic district.
  c. The ADU is part of the proposed or existing primary residence or an
  accessory structure under subsection 9-5.604(a)(1) above.
  d. When on-street parking permits are required but not offered to the
  occupant of the ADU.
  e. When there is an established car share vehicle stop located within one
  block of the ADU.
  f. When the permit application to create an ADU is submitted with an
  application to create a new single-family or new multifamily dwelling on the
  same lot, provided that the ADU or the lot satisfies any other criteria listed
  in subsections 9-5.606(g)(2)a through e above.
  g. When the resident or owner of an ADU does not operate or maintain an
  autoette pursuant to a valid resident vehicle permit, also referred to
  interchangeably as an autoette permit, pursuant to AMC Title 4, Chapter
  4-4 Traffic, Article 17 Registration of Vehicles.
  (3) No Replacement. When a garage, carport, or covered parking structure, or
  uncovered parking space is demolished in conjunction with the construction of an
  ADU or converted to an ADU, those off-street parking spaces are not required to
  be replaced.
(h) Architectural Requirements.
  (1) The materials and colors of the exterior walls, roof, and windows and doors
  must match the appearance and architectural design of those of the primary
  dwelling.
  (2) The exterior lighting must be limited to down-lights or as otherwise required
  by the building or fire code.
  (3) The ADU must have an independent exterior entrance, apart from that of the
  primary dwelling.
  (4) The interior horizontal dimensions of an ADU must be at least 10 feet wide in
  every direction, with a minimum interior wall height of seven feet.
  (5) No window or door of the ADU may have a direct line of sight to an adjoining
   residential property. Each window and door must either be located where there is
  no direct line of sight or screened using fencing, landscaping, or privacy glass to
  prevent a direct line of sight.
  (6) All windows and doors in an ADU are less than 30 feet from a property line
  that is not a public right-of-way line must either be (for windows) clerestory with
  the bottom of the glass at least six feet above the finished floor, or (for windows
  and for doors) utilize frosted or obscure glass.
  (7) The roof slope must match that of the dominant roof slope of the primary
  dwelling. The dominant roof slope is the slope shared by the largest portion of the
  roof.
(i) Landscape Requirements. Landscaping shall comply with the objective requirements
of the underlying zone.

(j) Allowed Stories. No ADU subject to this subsection 9-5.606 may have more than one
story, except that an ADU that is attached to the primary dwelling may have the stories
allowed under subsection 9-5.605(b)(4).

§ 9-5.607 Fees.
The following requirements apply to all ADU5 that are approved under subsections 9-
5.604(a) or 9-5.604(b) above.
(a) Impact Fees.
  (1) No impact fee is required for an ADU that is less than 750 square feet in size.
  For purposes of this subsection 9-5.607(a), “impact fee” means a “fee” under the
  Mitigation Fee Act (Gov. Code § 66000(b)) and a fee under the Quimby Act (Gov.
  Code § 66477). “Impact fee” here does not include any connection fee or capacity
  charge for water or sewer service.
  (2) Any impact fee that is required for an ADU that is 750 square feet or larger in
  size must be charged proportionately in relation to the square footage of the
  primary dwelling unit. (E.g., the floor area of the ADU, divided by the floor area of
  the primary dwelling, times the typical fee amount charged for a new dwelling.)
(b) Utility Fees.
  (1) If an ADU is constructed with a new single-family home, a separate utility
  connection directly between the ADU and the utility and payment of the normal
  connection fee and capacity charge for a new dwelling are required.
  (2) Except as described in subsection 9-5.607(b)(1), converted ADUs on a single
  family lot that are created under subsection 9-5.607(a)(1) above are not required
  to have a new or separate utility connection directly between the ADU and the
  utility. Nor is a connection fee or capacity charge required.
  (3) Except as described in subsection 9-5.607(b)(1), all ADU5 that are not
   covered by subsection 9-5.607(b)(2) require a new, separate utility connection
  directly between the ADU and the utility for any utility that is provided by the city.
  All utilities that are not provided by the city are subject to the connection and fee
  requirements of the utility provider.
  a. The connection is subject to a connection fee or capacity charge that is
  proportionate to the burden created by the ADU based on either the floor
  area or the number of drainage-fixture units (DFU) values, as defined by
  the Uniform Plumbing Code, upon the water or sewer system.
  b. The portion of the fee or charge that is charged by the City may not
  exceed the reasonable cost of providing this service.

§ 9-5.608 Nonconforming Zoning Code Conditions, Building Code Violations, and
Unpermitted Structures.
(a) Generally. The city will not deny an ADU or JADU application due to a nonconforming
zoning condition, building code violation, or unpermitted structure on the lot that does
not present a threat to the public health and safety and that is not affected by the
construction oftheADU 0rJADU.
(b) Unpermitted ADU5 constructed before 2020.
  (1) Permit to Legalize. As required by state law, the city may not deny a permit to
  legalize an existing but unpermitted ADU that was constructed before January 1,
  2020, if denial is based on either of the following grounds:
  a. The ADU violates applicable building standards, or
  b. The ADU does not comply with the state ADU law (Government
  Code section 65852.2) or this ADU ordinance (AMC 9-5.6).
  (2) Exceptions:
  a. Notwithstanding subsection 9-5.608(b)(1) above, the City may deny a
  permit to legalize an existing but unpermitted ADU that was constructed
  before January 1, 2020, if the City makes a finding that correcting a
  violation is necessary to comply with the standards specified in California
  Health and Safety Code section 17920.3.
  b. Subsection 9-5.608(b)(1) above does not apply to a building that is
  deemed to be substandard in accordance with California Health and
  Safety Code section 17920.3.

§ 9-5.609 Nonconforming ADUs and Discretionary Approval.
Any proposed ADU or JADU that would otherwise be allowed under this this section but
does not conform to the objective standards set forth in subsections 9-5.601 through 9-
5.608 of this section may be allowed by the City with a conditional use permit, in
accordance with the other provisions of this title.

for the professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental Solutions, Inc., to
continue to provide cultural resource consulting for the Five Corner Site Improvement
Project, for an additional sum of $50,000 and a new total contract sum of $216,128.00.

REPORT SUMMARY: On November 25, 2024 the City of Avalon issued a notice to
proceed to Jordahl Construction, Inc. to complete the Five Corners Site Improvement
Project (CIP Project #180003).

Knowing a portion of the scope of work essential for this project was being completed in
a designated culturally sensitive area, the City planned to contract with a cultural resource
consultant to provide on call oversight. On December 16, 2024, the City entered into a
professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental Solutions, Inc. (Montrose)
to provide on-call cultural resources consultation services for a not to exceed sum of
$24,000.

Shortly after contracting with Montrose, archeologists on site noted potentially culturally
significant items being excavated through the eastern edge of Tremont Street between
Catalina and Clarissa Avenues. After an initial assessment of the site, Montrose provided
a revised proposal outlining a scope of services to provide cultural resource monitoring
services and sediment screening as well as a final monitoring report for a total of
$117,889.

On January 21, 2025, the City Council authorized the City Manager to negotiate and enter
into a professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental Services, Inc. to
provide cultural resource consulting for the Five Corners Site Improvement Project for a
not to exceed sum of $118,000.

On April 17,2025, Montrose provided City Staff with Change Order #1. This change order
expanded Montrose’s monitoring time on site until September 2025. Initially, monitoring
efforts were projected to continue from December 2024 through the end of March 2025.
However, due to an expanded project schedule as well as the discovery of cultural
 findings within the project area, Montrose and City Staff saw the need to expand the
monitoring timeline.

On October 10, 2025, Montrose requested the City authorize Change Order #2
authorizing an additional $50,000 to the contract sum. This change order will expand
Montrose’s monitoring efforts through December 2025 to coincide with the completion of
the excavation phases of the project. Additionally, the change order provides additional
scope to support the coordination of repatriation of cultural resources discovered
throughout the project.

If approved, the total contract sum for Montrose to provide Cultural Resources
Consultation will increase to $216,128. The costs of this contractwill be allocated to Fiscal
Year 25-26 Capital Improvement Program Project #180003, account #10575-6547.

SUBJECT:  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent
  Control Measures

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control
options available under State law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (‘City”) staff to
evaluate and report back on any desired local options available to the City.

REPORT SUMMARY: The purpose of this staff report is to provide the City Council with
information on State law as it relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide
examples of what other cities have codified locally so the City Council may consider what
policy options it is interested in exploring for Avalon. The Tenant Protection Act of 2019
provides the statewide baseline for tenant protections. That baseline can be raised by the City,
as long as it is done in compliance with Costa-Hawkins, which places limits on the kinds of
tenant protections a locality may adopt.

  I.  City of Avalon’s Municipal Code and Existing Tenant Protections
The City currently has no specific provisions in the Avalon Municipal Code (“AMC”) that impose
City-created rent control (also known as “rent stabilization”). Chapter 9-1 1 of the AMC includes
City-specific Affordable Housing requirements. The purpose of Chapter 9-1 1 is meant to
“[e]ncourage the availability of dignified, safe, and affordable workforce housing within the City
of Avalon by promoting development of decent living environments and removing unnecessary
barriers to such development.” (AMC 9-11.101(c).) This includes a City inclusionary housing
requirement to construct a percentage of affordable housing as part of any new residential
development. Specifically, for any new residential development creating five or more for-sale or
rental units, developers are required to set aside at least 20% of those units at an affordable
rent or cost (pursuant to State income limits). However, these City requirements are only
applicable to new commercial or residential development, and do not provide tenant protections
or affordability controls for existing housing stock.

  II.  State Law: The Tenant Protection Act of 2019 and Its Subsequent Changes

A.  2019 Framework, the Tenant Protection Act
In 2019, the State Legislature approved and the Governor signed Assembly Bill 1482, the
Tenant Protection Act (the “Act”). The Act set the “floor” with a series of new tenant protection
measures that must be followed by all California landlords. However, cities can go above that
“floor” in setting more protective local controls for its tenants.
 The Act broadly prevents landlords from terminating or declining to renew leases with tenants
of at least a year without ‘just cause,” as defined under California Civil Code section 1946.2.
“Just cause” is divided into two categories, “no-fault” termination and “at-fault” termination,
which each have their own eligibility criteria and protections for tenants. The information below
is meant to provide a non-exhaustive summary of the provisions under the Act. Importantly,
when a landlord evicts a tenant under no-fault just cause, the landlord must pay relocation
assistance equal to one-month’s rent, regardless of tenant income1. As described in additional
detail below, a number of cities have required more significant relocation benefits than one-
month, and expanded the types of evictions eligible for relocation benefits.

  •  No-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, withdrawal of the unit from the
  rental market; or an intent to demolish or “substantially remodel” the residential
  property.
  a The definition of a “substantial remodel” that qualifies as a no-fault termination
  includes:
  when the remodel “cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner”
  with the tenant present, and requires the tenant to vacate for at least 30
  consecutive days, and either:
  • (1) replacement or substantial modification of any structural,
  electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit; or
  • (2) the abatement of hazardous materials.

  •  At-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, instances where tenant is in default
  on rent; breach of any material term of the lease (generally after landlord issues a
  written notice to correct); and a nuisance as defined under State law (including unlawful
  possession of weapons and the manufacture, cultivation, or possession for sale of
  controlled substances).

The Act also includes a statewide “floor” of rent control. Specifically, State law limits rent
increases over a 12-month period, with a maximum increase of no more than 5% plus the
percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (“CPI”), or 10% percent, whichever is
lower.

It is important to note there are a series of exemptions from the applicability of the Act written
into State law. Specifically, certain housing types that are not subject to State law tenant
protections, which include: affordable housing restricted by deed or subject to existing rent or
price controls; dormitories; single-family, owner-occupied residences; housing less than 15
years old; and some mobilehomes.

B.  State Law Amendments Strengthening the Act (SB 567)

 Senate Bill 567, which became operative on April 1, 2024, tightened the rules for no-fault just
cause evictions, substantial remodels and rent increases. SB 567 created stricter enforcement
rules to reduce the ability of landlords to evict tenants and then rent out the unit at market rate.

For an eviction by the landlord because the landlord or their family member will be moving into
a dwelling unit with an existing tenant (a type of no-fault just cause eviction), the landlord or
family member must not already live on the property or have access to another vacant unit on
the property. The landlord or family member also must move in within 90 days of the tenant
moving out, and stay in the unit for at least a year. Tenants have the right to know the
relationship of any family member who is moving in, and can request proof. A vacating tenant
is also given the opportunity to move back in at the same rent rate, along with moving
expenses, if the landlord or family member does not move in within the specified timeframe or
fails to stay for the full year.

For substantial remodels, landlords must provide a detailed notice outlining the work to be
done, any necessary permits, and inform tenants that they can return to their units if the work
is not completed or if they do not need to vacate during certain days.

Regarding the Act’s rent control provisions, SB 567 introduced penalties for landlords who
collect rent above the maximum allowed, based on the rent amount that was overcharged, that
may also include attorneys’ fees and court costs. A landlord may also be penalized up to three
times the amount of charged rent, if they acted willfully or with malice. They may also be liable
for damages. These new laws did not change the existing law on rent control or
allowable rent increases under the Act.

 It is important to note that as a general rule, the State-adopted Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing
Act (“Costa-Hawkins”) limits the extent to which cities and counties can enact rent control or
rent stabilization ordinances. Specifically, the City of Avalon could only adopt a rent control
measure that applies to apartments that received their certificate of occupancy before
February 1, 1995. Tenant protections therefore generally cannot be applied to single family
homes or condominiums unless a limited exception to Costa-Hawkins applies (e.g. owned by a
corporation, real estate investment trust, or an LLC with corporate ownership). Costa Hawkins
allows only the owner/landlord, and not local government, to set the rental rates for units that
received certificates of occupancy after February 1, j9952 Additionally, cities and counties
can legislate only on the allowed percentage of rental increases as to existing tenants,
and may not limit the initial rental rate to new tenants except under limited circumstances.
Cities and counties can regulate initial rental rates if (1) the tenancy was terminated with 30 or
60-day notice or due to a change in the terms of the tenancy other than those permitted by
law, (2) the landlord terminates or fails to renew a contract or recorded agreement for a rent
limitation with a government agency, or (3) the regulation is to permit tenants with permanent
physical disabilities to move to accessible units and the property being regulated is already
subject to the local rent control ordinance.3 For those reasons, in all the cities and counties
with rent control ordinances that are described below, any time a tenant voluntarily moves out,
the landlord is permitted to set the new rent without restriction, based on the new tenancy.

C.  New California Laws with Additional Tenant Protections
There are two, additional new laws aimed at improving housing security and protecting tenants
from unfair evictions and rent increases that are described briefly below.

  •  AB 12 and AB 2801: Limits the security deposit landlords can collect after July 1,
  2024, to a maximum of one month’s rent, regardless of whether the rental
  property is furnished or unfurnished. An exception is made for “small property”
  owners that are natural persons or limited liability companies where all members
  are natural persons and own no more than two residential rental properties
  comprising of four or fewer units. This exception does not apply to security
  deposits for active service members.

  •  AB 1418: Prevents local governments from adopting regulations that encourage
  evicting tenants based on calls to law enforcement, alleged criminal activity, or
  other alleged nuisances. AB 1418 also prohibits local governments from requiring
  or encouraging landlords to conduct criminal background checks when screening
  tenants. Additionally, local governments are prohibited from enacting an
  ordinance that defines a nuisance as contact with law enforcement.

  •  AB 2347: Gives tenants five additional days to respond to a notice of unlawful
  detainer (eviction notice).

  •  AB 2493: Prohibits landlords from charging application screening fees when they
  know or should know that no rental units are available. A landlord can only
  charge an application screening fee if the landlord uses an application screening
  process that complies with certain statutory requirements.

  •  AB 2801: Limits the claims that a landlord can bring against a tenant for restoring
  a property to what is necessary to return the property to its pre-tenancy condition.
  Beginning on July 1, 2025, landlords must take photographs of a rental unit at the
  beginning and end of the tenancy to show the need for any repairs or cleanings
  that the tenant is charged for.

  •  SB 267: Prohibits the use of an applicant’s credit history as part of the application
  process for a rental housing accommodation without offering alternative options
  for verifying the applicant’s ability to pay rent.

  •  SB 611: Prohibits charging tenants fees for using checks to pay rent or security
  deposits or for delivering a notice of termination. If a tenant is a military service
  member and is charged a higher than standard amount for a security deposit, the
  landlord must provide a written explanation of the need for a higher amount and
   return the additional amount to the tenant after 6 months if the tenant is not in
  arrears for any rent.

  Ill. Examples of Tenant Protection and Rent Control Actions Taken by Other Cities

The City Council may provide direction to codify requirements set out under State law so
Avalon may take local, administrative enforcement action, including issuing administrative
citations that include City approved penalty amounts, or adding local civil or criminal remedies.
The City Council may also provide direction for City staff to evaluate  for possible future

for what may be of interest to Avalon. All tenant protections listed below are permissible
under the Costa-Hawkins Act.

A majority of the cities cited below are charter cities. Charter cities have greater authority to
govern themselves than a general law city, like Avalon. However, and as described above, the
Tenant Protection Act and related State laws provide the “floor,” not the ceiling. State law
allows local tenant protection and/or rent control ordinances so long as they provide the same
or better protections for tenants, with corresponding findings that the local ordinance is both
consistent and “more protective” than State law. This is true for both charter cities and general
law cities.

Accordingly, should Council provide direction to evaluate rent control in the City of Avalon, the
City’s ordinance can be more protective than the “floor” set out under the Act, should ensure a
process by which landlords can petition (appeal) the City to increase the otherwise allowable
rent increase for a fair return of investment, and finally, upon direction, our office will ensure
the proposed local ordinance is otherwise consistent and not preempted by any State or
Federal law (including Costa-Hawkins)  . Any adopted ordinance should also evidence the
City’s interest in promoting long-term stability and certainty for renters, in addition to any other
Avalon-specific public purposes.

Whatever direction the City Council provides, City staff will work with the City Attorney’s Office
to ensure any proposed policy change on tenant protections and/or rent control that come back
to the City Council are vetted consistent with State law.

A.  Examples of Locally-adopted Rent ControllRent Stabilization Ordinances

  •  Culver City. Culver City has adopted a series of more expansive rent control and
  tenant protections than under State law. For relocation assistance, Culver City requires
  a relocation fee to be the greater of three times the tenant’s current monthly rent or an
  amount established U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”)
  formula that is based on fair market rent.

  Culver City does not allow no-fault just cause eviction when the tenant is 62 years or
  older, is disabled or terminally ill, is a qualifying low-income tenant under State income
   limits, or when the tenant has school-aged children who are protected from eviction
  during the school year term.

  Culver City caps annual rent increases at no more than 5% annually. However, if the
  percentage change to the consumer price index (‘CPI”) on an annual basis is less than
  2%, rent increases in Culver City may not exceed 2% that year. If CPI is greater than
  5%, the annual 5% cap still applies and no increase may exceed that percentage.
  There are exemptions, including but not limited to, when State or Federal law expressly
  exempts the unit from price control and when the landlord receives government
  subsidies for the unit. Importantly, Culver City’s rent control measures apply only to
  otherwise eligible units that received their certificate of occupancy before February 1,
  1995. This threshold date is within local rent control measures, since it is controlled
  under State law (see discussion above on Costa-Hawkins).

  Similar to other cities and regulations discussed in additional detail below, landlords
  may petition the city if they believe the rent control regulations prevent them from
  earning a fair return on their property investment.

  For no-fault terminations, such as property demolition or when a landlord or their
  relative is moving in, Culver City requires landlords to pay relocation assistance. This
  amount is typically three times the monthly rent plus an additional $1,000. Small
  landlords, defined as those owning three or fewer units, are required to pay less.
  Landlords can deduct any past due rent from the relocation payment.

  Landlords in Culver City must also register their rental units annually with the city, and

Legal Framework
Though the use of medical cannabis was legalized in the State of California in 1996, adult-use
or recreational cannabis was prohibited until adoption of Proposition 64 on November 8, 2016.
On June 27, 2017, Governor Jerry Brown signed into law a single comprehensive legislative
document that took the existing regulatory framework established for medical cannabis and
incorporated non-medical cannabis regulations. This legislation is known as the Medicinal and
Adult-Use Cannabis Regulation and Safety Act (‘MAUCRSA”). The legislation specifically
preserved local jurisdictional authority to adopt and enforce local ordinances that limit or
completely prohibit the establishment or operation of medical and non-medical cannabis
business operations within their purview. The state licensing authority will not approve an
application for a state cannabis business license if the state license will violate a local
ordinance in the jurisdiction it will operate.

The Department of Cannabis Control Medicinal and Adult-Use Commercial Cannabis
Regulations  —  California Code of Regulations Title 4 Division 19 Section §15311,
‘Requirements for the Transportation of Cannabis and Cannabis ProdLicts” establishes the
  —

requirements for transporting cannabis and cannabis products between licensees or licensed
premises.

Though regulation §153111 (e) expressly prohibits transportation of cannabis and cannabis
products “by means of aircraft, watercraft, drone, rail, human-powered vehicle, or unstaffed
vehicle,” a carve out exits for Catalina within Section (p):

  Notwithstanding subsection (e), transportation of cannabis and cannabis products may
  be conducted via wate,way to licensees located on Catalina Island. The provisions of
  this section and other sections regarding vehicle requirements also apply to vessels
   used to transport cannabis and cannabis products via waterway pursuant to this
  section

Cannabis is an illegal substance under the Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 USC et.
seq., (“Act”) which makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate, manufacture, distribute or
dispense, or possess with intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense cannabis. The Act does
not contain any exemption for cannabis used for medical purposes. Additionally, per federal
law, cannabis is listed as a Schedule 1 drug. Federal penalties for possession of cannabis
include:
  -  First Offense  —  Misdemeanor with potential for up to one year of incarceration and
  $1  000 in fines.
  -  Second Offense  — Misdemeanor punishable by 15 days to two years of incarceration
  and $2,500 in fines.
  -  Third and subsequent Offenses  — Misdemeanor or felony punishable by 90 days to 3
  years of incarceration and fines up to $2,500.

Federal penalties increase significantly for selling or attempting to sell cannabis based on the
amount:
  -  Less than 50 kilograms  Felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a
  —

  $250,000 fine
  -  50 to 99 kilograms Felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison and fines of up to
  —

  $1,000,000.
  -  100 to 999 kilograms  Felony punishable by five to 40 years in prison and possible
  —

  fines of up to $2,000,000.
  -  1000 kg and up  —Felony punishable by ten years to life in prison and $4,000,000 in
  fines.

However, it should be noted, federal law enforcement agencies have issued guidelines
allowing for state regulatory policies that include cannabis for medical purposes. Specifically,
the Rohrabaher-Farr Amendment, first introduced to the U.S. House of Representatives in
2001 and adopted in an omnibus spending bill in December 2014, prohibits the U.S. Justice
Department from spending any funds on actions designed to interfere with the state medical
cannabis laws. To date, this provision has been included in every subsequent spending bill.

Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment states:

  None of the funds made available in this Act to the Department of Justice may be used,
  with respect to the States of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado,
  Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Kentucky,
  Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana,
  Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, South
  Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin, to prevent such
  States from implementing their own State laws that authorize the use, distribution,
  possession, or cultivation of medical manjuana.
 The Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment is vitally important for the City of Avalon’s medical
cannabis program as the surrounding Pacific Ocean falls within the jurisdictional authority of
the United States Coast Guard (‘USCG”).

The City has received reports of medical cannabis delivery vessels being boarded by USCG.
As the vessel, medical cannabis and medical cannabis products have had all of the required
documentation for certified medical use, no action was taken by the USCG. The Harbormaster
contacted the USCG who confirmed, adult-use cannabis transportation in federal waterways is
illegal.

Though, state regulation §153111 (p) does not distinguish between medical or adult-use
cannabis in is regulatory carve out for Catalina Island, the Rohrahacher-Farr Amendment is
specific in its guidance to restrict funding for interference with State permitted medical
cannabis operations. No federal protections, exemptions or guidelines exist for adult-
use/recreational cannabis. When state law and federal law conflict, federal law displaces or
preempts state law. Therefore, City Staff interpret there is no viable way to transport adult-use
cannabis to Catalina Island without violating federal law (transportation of a controlled
substance) and/or risking the federal penalties as described within this report.

The Department of Justice has proposed a rule change to move cannabis from Schedule I to
Schedule Ill controlled substance. The rule change emphasizes the currently accepted medical
use of cannabis, but, again, does not address adult use. If the rule change occurs,
transportation of cannabis across federal waterways will still be prohibited.

Development of Local Cannabis Regulations and Public Interest in Adult-Use Cannabis

After the establishment of state-wide legislation regarding cannabis, acting in accordance with
its local jurisdictional authority under MAUCRSA, the Avalon City Council began the process to
develop its local ordinance. After discussions and code revisions at four City Council meetings,
the current cannabis ordinance (Ordinance #1163-17, Chapter 5-20 of the AMC) was adopted
on November 7, 2017.

In development of Ordinance #1163-17, the City Council worked to provide a means for public

SUBJECT:  206 E. Whittley Retaining Wall Change Order

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute a first
amendment to the construction contract between the City of Avalon and Jordahi Construction
Inc. incorporating Change Order #1 and increasing the contract sum by $270,000 for a total not
to exceed amount of $987,255. 2. Amend the Fiscal Year 25-26 Budget by allocating an
additional $170,000 to Capital Improvement Project #205015, Fund #15325-6547.

REPORT SUMMARY: A multi-family property at 206 E. Whittley was purchased by the ACIA in
2008 with the intent to provide affordable housing units. In July 2019, the City Council, acting
as the Housing Authority, approved final construction plans to renovate the structure.

In preparation of the total construction project, local contractors completed improvements to the
sewer lateral and water lines from East Whittley to the property. As a result of this effort all
utilities are onsite and at the needed capacity for the existing and the proposed additional
building.

In developing the plan for a potential second building, geotechnical engineers determined the
existing retaining walls at the property’s boundaries need remediation to extend their service life
in the case of the existing building or replacement in the case of the new building, due to
corrosion on the existing tiebacks and age of the concrete.

In order to ensure the opportunity for highest and best use of the property, Staff proposed
remediation of the existing retaining wall, and additionally leveling and backfilling of an adjacent
area that will widen and recapture areas of the southern portion of the East Whittley public right-
of-way at the 90-degree curve. The elevation and further frontage improvements of the right-of-
way will allow for on-site parking for all nine (9) future housing units (four in the original building
and up to five in the new structure) and also provide three additional public parking spaces on
East Whittley. Additionally, the new site plan will repurpose the existing on-street parking area
and provide a convenient stopping/loading/unloading area for large delivery or trash vehicles in
the roadway, as well as provide better emergency access/staging. While this widening will
reduce one informal unmaintained access to the back of the Hermosa Hotel, the primary access
point at the “Museum” public stairway will continue to provide a safe direct connection to the
upper rear walkway of the Hermosa complex. This access point will be further improved with the
project.

A Request for Proposals to perform necessary site preparation work as well as construct the a
retaining wall was issued on May 2, 2023.
 Due to the complexity of the project and the formal bid requirements the project bid opening was
extended until June 27, 2023. On June 27, 2023, the City Council, acting as the Housing
Authority, held a Special Meeting to adopt a resolution rejecting the bids received and authorizing
the City Manager to negotiate a contract with Jordahl Construction, Inc. A contract with Jordahl
Construction, Inc. was executed on June 29, 2023 for a total not to exceed sum of $717,255.00.

Jordahl Construction, Inc. has been working diligently on this project. However, while working
on the lower extent of the westerly side of the property it was determined the existing lower
retaining wall at the property line did not have the required structural support for the proposed
MSE retaining wall. In order to move forward, without impacting the Hermosa Hotel property,
City Staff and Jordahl Construction, Inc. have redesigned the footing of the wall to stay well
within the property boundaries. This redesign effort has resulted in Change Order #1 from
Jordahl Construction, Inc. This change order proposes a modification in contract scope of
$441 ,240; however, the net result to the contract is offset by portions of work not completed due
to this change in condition. This offset will result in an approximate contract savings of $171,318.
If approved, Change Order #1 will increase the contract with Jordahl Construction, Inc., by
$270,000 resulting in a final contract sum of $987,255.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Infrastructure reliability and safety. Affordable housing availability.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Amend the Fiscal Year 25-26 Budget will be amended by allocating an
additional $170,000 to Capital Improvement Project #20515, Fund #15325-6547.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not be able
to utilize the entire parcel at its highest and best use. The expenditure of these funds will directly
impact the availability of affordable housing.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.
